title: Water for both sides
told: a sakhi of Bhai Ghanaiya, a traditional story

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever helped someone you didn’t really like?
options: then you’ve already started today’s lesson. listen.
that’s honest. listen to one old man.

steps.line: In Guru Gobind Singh’s time, during the battles at Anandpur, wounded and thirsty soldiers lay in the dust on both sides.
steps.label: a traditional story

steps.line: An old Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya walked among them with a leather water bag, giving each one a drink.
He gave water to everyone. Sikh soldiers, and the enemy’s soldiers too.

steps.q: Some Sikhs see him giving water to the enemy. What do you think they do?
o: Bring him to the Guru, angry
steps.why: They were angry, and took him straight to the Guru.

steps.line: Some Sikhs were angry. They brought him to Guru Gobind Singh. He’s helping the enemy!

steps.q: What do you think Ghanaiya tells the Guru?
o: He saw no enemy, only you in every face
He couldn’t tell one side from the other
He was only doing what he was told
steps.why: He saw no friend or enemy. Only the Guru’s light in every face.

steps.line: Ghanaiya answered: I don’t see friend or enemy. I see you in every face.
The Guru was pleased. He gave Ghanaiya a soothing balm. Keep giving water, he said, and ease their wounds too.

steps.q: Why did the Guru give him a balm instead of stopping him?
o: To keep him away from the fighting
To reward him with a fine gift
To say: care for everyone, enemy too
steps.why: The Guru didn’t just allow it. He asked for more of it. Care has no sides.

steps.line: Today, Sikhs end their standing prayer, the Ardas, with three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Today many Sikhs call Bhai Ghanaiya a forerunner of what?
steps.why: More than 150 years before the Red Cross, he tended the wounded of both sides. Sikh volunteer groups still carry that spirit into disaster and war zones.

steps.q: Ghanaiya’s work is called seva. What makes seva different from just helping?
o: It earns a place in heaven
steps.why: Seva is selfless service, done without wanting reward. Sikhs practice it everywhere, from the langar kitchen to cleaning shoes at the gurdwara door.

say: here’s what i love. ghanaiya didn’t check sides before he poured. he saw a thirsty person.
sikhs carry that in the ardas. after remembering the gurus and the five beloved, the prayer ends with sarbat da bhala, the good of all. as if to say, “not just us.”

steps.q: Ghanaiya saw the Guru in every face. If he’s right, who is left out of “the good of all”?
o: Only those who fight against you
steps.why: Nobody. If the Guru’s light is in every face, nobody falls outside “all.” That’s why he could pour for both sides.

today.say: if you like, try a tiny piece of it with me: stand for a breath, palms together, and wish one person well, then someone you find hard to wish well. watch, learn, or join in. it’s your choice.
options: the good of all. that’s the whole prayer, really.
that counts too. ghanaiya started with one cup.

Ardas closing words: “Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala” (Sikh Rehat Maryada, text of Ardas)
